predictions: There will be no reproducible allele-specific TF occupancy that causes a TF-dependent change in TERT expression in relevant tumor cells.

chains.title: Possible alt-allele gain of ETS-family binding, with GABPA as a candidate

links.claim: The QBiC-SELEX result predicts greater alt-allele binding, but its best model is ETV5-mapped and gives the same result for several ETS factors; it does not identify GABPA specifically. GABPA is a candidate because it has variant-overlapping peaks in other biosamples and is expressed in the stated context, but occupancy in glioblastoma is not established.
The variant lies in a promoter-like cCRE with chromatin activity indicated by maxima across ENCODE biosamples, not specifically in glioblastoma cells.
The promoter location makes altered TERT regulation plausible, but the supplied evidence does not show that GABPA or ETS binding at this variant changes TERT expression.

This is proposed for glioblastoma cells; GABPA is expressed in the stated context, but no matching-context occupancy is shown, and the U-87 MG query found no peak while noting that an experiment may be absent.

A TERT regulatory effect could be relevant to TERT-promoter-associated melanoma and IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, but the supplied evidence does not establish this mechanism or its contribution to bladder cancer.

predictions: In relevant tumor cells, the alt allele should show greater occupancy by GABPA or another ETS factor at this site.
A TERT expression difference caused by editing the allele should be reduced by perturbing the ETS factor that actually occupies the site.
falsified_if: Relevant tumor cells show no allele-dependent ETS occupancy at this site.
Isogenic allele editing produces no reproducible ETS-dependent change in TERT expression.

chains.title: Possible ref-allele gain of CTCF binding at the TERT promoter

links.claim: CTCF's own QBiC-SELEX model predicts stronger binding to the ref allele; a variant-overlapping CTCF peak is reported in another biosample, not in glioblastoma cells.
The variant lies in a promoter-like cCRE, but the reported chromatin maxima do not establish activity in glioblastoma cells.
The promoter location makes a TERT effect plausible, but no supplied evidence connects CTCF binding at this site to TERT expression or determines the direction of any effect.
CTCF is expressed in the stated context, but the reported occupancy is from another biosample and does not demonstrate binding in glioblastoma cells.

A TERT regulatory effect could be relevant to TERT-promoter-associated melanoma and IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, but this CTCF mechanism is not demonstrated and the supplied literature does not establish relevance to bladder cancer.

predictions: If CTCF occupies this site in relevant tumor cells, occupancy should be greater on the ref allele.
Any allele-dependent TERT regulatory effect attributed to this chain should be reduced by disrupting CTCF.
falsified_if: CTCF does not occupy the site in relevant tumor cells.
The ref allele does not show greater CTCF occupancy, or CTCF perturbation leaves the allele-dependent TERT effect unchanged.

next_experiment: The top two hypotheses are H1 and H0. The cheapest informative test is a dual-allele TERT-promoter reporter assay in a glioblastoma cell model, measuring reporter output with and without GABPA depletion. H1 predicts an allele-dependent output difference reduced by GABPA depletion; H0 predicts no reproducible GABPA-dependent allele effect. This is a screening test and would not replace validation at the endogenous locus.

A major molecular feature of melanoma is abnormal telomerase activation; this is most often caused by telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) promoter mutations, which occur in 50-82% of cases and are the most common noncoding alteration in this cancer.

Conclusions: Understanding both telomere-dependent and -independent TERT functions is essential for developing effective biomarkers and therapies that overcome resistance and slow melanoma progression.
The genetic landscape of familial melanoma is heterogeneous.
CDKN2A and CDK4 mutations act through UV-dependent and cell cycle disruption pathways, while BAP1, POT1, and TERT mutations are considered UV-independent.
BackgroundMutations in the telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) promoter region (TPM), particularly C228T and C250T, are common in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma (GBM).

ConclusionThe rs2853669 C allele may increase GBM susceptibility and, when in cis with TPM, is associated with reduced TERT expression and poorer prognosis, underscoring its biological and clinical significance in TPM-mutant GBM.
Additionally, loss of either USP10 or FOXM1 suppresses the expression of the downstream target Telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT), triggering cellular senescence.

TERT promoter (TERTp) mutations are among the most frequent molecular alterations in isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) wild-type glioblastoma (GBM), yet the molecular profiles and prognostic implications associated with TERTp status remain incompletely characterized.
The prognostic relevance of CDKN2A deletion may vary according to TERTp status, particularly for OS.
